children: As fall arrives and a new generation of financial advisors enters the workforce, it's a good time to step back and ask: What truly drives long-term success in wealth management?

Young professionals of all stripes have always felt the pressure to get everything right from the start-to land the ideal job, make smart career moves, and stay ahead of the competition. That's particularly true in finance where the headlines, volatility, and constant noise can make it seem as though success comes from perfect timing or reacting faster than everyone else.

But after decades in the industry-first as a young broker at Merrill Lynch and then as the owner of a retirement planning firm-I've learned a simple truth: Those who thrive aren't always the smartest or most talented; they're the ones who earn client trust one conversation at a time.

Early in my career, a client referred me to three family members-not because I delivered the highest investment returns, but because I returned every phone call and followed through on every commitment. Years later, I worked with a widow who was overwhelmed after losing her husband. By listening carefully, guiding her through each step, and simply being there during a difficult time, she became one of my strongest advocates and has referred dozens of people to me over the years.

Building trust. Today's advisors are digitally fluent, innovative, and eager to learn. Yet many have not had enough opportunities to develop the relationship-building skills that become increasingly important as careers progress.

Recently, I've watched a young advisor in our office build a thriving practice, not through aggressive sales tactics, but by consistently putting clients first. When the advisor got a call about a client's job loss, they didn't text back details on how to roll over the old 401(k). Rather, they took the time to call the client and hear the concern in their voice. Only then did the advisor suggest the rollover and walk the client through the steps-and then explain how to post a résumé to LinkedIn for good measure! The actions made a huge impact on the client.

At my firm we preach over and over that while artificial intelligence can improve efficiency, it is no replacement for caring about clients. I have seen how exercising empathy and treating others as we want to be treated is key to building a better book of business. I've seen how it preserves advisor-client relationships through rough markets-much more than a hot investment tip ever does.

The habits that create trust might seem simple: keep your word, listen attentively, treat people with respect, follow through on commitments, and make others feel heard. Yet these behaviors compound quietly and powerfully over time, creating credibility that opens doors. In a world increasingly shaped by automation, artificial intelligence, and rapid change, the human element is becoming more valuable, not less.

Michael Oana is the founder of Michael Oana Retirement Planning Specialist in Columbia, South Carolina. He is a Certified Retirement Counselor. His book, The Financial Advisor's Guide to Building Trust, was published last spring.
